catalog_quote: Forster 1963 pp.19-20: "2. Contrastive features of pitch, stress, and length occur on polysyllabic roots of Dibabawon. Any of these features may be modified by intonation... 2.1 On utterances having unmodified statement intonation, high pitch occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable. This is true in isolated or "list" words and also in longer utterances. ... 2.2 Primary stress falls on the final or penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word. Since speakers of American English tend to "hear" louder stress on any syllable which carries relatively higher pitch, the fact that high pitch consistently occurs on the penultimate syllable of any utterance having unmodified statement intonation gives the impression that primary stress always occurs there also. While in fact primary stress is more common on the penultimate than on the final syllable of Dibabawon utterances, there are examples…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation from Forster 1963 pp.19-20 is verbatim in the PDF we hold/text layer and on the held p.20 page image; the secondary-stress and p.24-25 statements are also there. (2) The classification rests on a 1963 primary phonology article by the language's principal fieldworker; it explicitly distinguishes contrastive word stress (final ~ penult, penult more frequent, minimal pair 'sa.kit/sa.'kit) from predictable utterance-penult high pitch, which is exactly the distinction the record uses to overrule the earlier phrase-level screen based on the 1987 texts intro. Glottolog (16 refs, none a grammar; Forster 1963 the only phonology), SIL archives (11 items, same picture) and a web search show no later grammar, phonology, dissertation or instrumental study of Dibabawon; the 1987 SIL texts volume itself refers readers to Forster 1963.
